title: A committed fourfold increase in ocean oxygen loss
problem: The full extent of future ocean oxygen loss already locked in by historical CO2 emissions is poorly quantified, obscuring the unavoidable, long-term impact on deep-ocean ecosystems that will persist even if global warming is halted.
method: The study employs an emission-driven Earth system model of intermediate complexity to conduct millennial-scale simulations assuming zero CO₂ emissions from year 2021 onwards, thereby quantifying the committed long-term changes in ocean oxygen levels caused by historical emissions.
task: The task is to quantify the committed, long-term ocean deoxygenation from historical CO2 emissions by using an Earth system model to simulate a future where all anthropogenic emissions stop from the year 2021 onwards.

innovation: This paper uses model simulations to demonstrate that historical CO₂ emissions have already committed the global ocean to a future oxygen loss more than three times larger than what has been realized to date, with this deoxygenation occurring predominantly in the deep ocean.

kg_extraction_triplets.paragraph: Model configuration. The University of Victoria Earth System Climate Model21, version 2.8, is employed in the configuration described in ref. 31. The ocean component is a fully three-dimensional primitive-equation model with 19 levels in the vertical ranging from 50 m near the surface to 500 m in the deep. It contains a simple marine ecosystem model including the two major nutrients, nitrate and phosphate, and two phytoplankton classes, nitrogen fixers and other phytoplankton, the former being limited by phosphate only.

kg_extraction_triplets.paragraph: The ocean component is coupled to a single-level energy-moisture balance model of the atmosphere, a dynamic-thermodynamic sea ice component, and a terrestrial vegetation and carbon-cycle component. Continental ice sheets are prescribed and kept fixed in the present configuration. All model components use a common horizontal resolution of 1.8° latitude times 3.6° longitude.

kg_extraction_triplets.paragraph: A metabolic index38 defined as the ratio of O2 supply to the temperature-dependent resting O2 demand of marine animals (until now sufficient information is available predominantly for upper ocean animals and it remains to be shown whether similar parameters can be confirmed experimentally for deep-sea animals39,40; see “Methods”) and indicator of metabolically viable marine environments, declines by 10% to 25% over much of the deep ocean below 2000 m between year 2020 and 2650 (Fig. 5).

A major deep-convection event in the Southern Ocean after year 2650 sets off a substantial release of heat and CO2 from the ocean to the atmosphere and surface air temperatures rise abruptly by 0.4 °C within 50 years.

The Atlantic shows little changes and, in some regions, even an oxygen increase due to the slowly increasing ventilation via the formation of North Atlantic Deep Water and the strengthening meridional overturning circulation (contours in Fig. 2h).
